lead: A differential amplifier has two inputs. The signal of interest is their difference; the average is often interference. Splitting the inputs into a difference vid and a common-mode average vicm lets us define two gains: differential gain Ad, which we want large, and common-mode gain Acm, which we want small. CMRR compares them. The idea is used in sensor front ends, ECG amplifiers, current sensing and every op-amp input stage.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for the matched pair and the small-signal models from Unit 2.

sections.h3: Difference and average of two inputs

blocks.text: Take two input voltages v1 and v2, both measured with respect to ground. Their difference is vid = v1 − v2. Their average is vicm = (v1 + v2)/2. The same pair can be rebuilt as v1 = vicm + vid/2 and v2 = vicm − vid/2. Here vid is the differential-mode input, in volts; vicm is the common-mode input, in volts. A differential amplifier should multiply vid by Ad and vicm by Acm. The output is the sum of these two contributions. The split matters because a wanted sensor signal usually appears as a difference, while mains hum, ground bounce and temperature drift often appear equally at both inputs, so they are common mode.

items: Measure v1 and v2 with ground as reference.
Rebuild the inputs as vicm plus or minus vid/2.

blocks.where: v1 and v2 are input voltages in V; vid is the differential-mode input in V; vicm is the common-mode input in V.

blocks.text: For a single-ended output at one collector, call the output voltage vo, in volts. Then vo = Ad vid + Acm vicm, where Ad = vo/vid is the differential-mode gain and Acm = vo/vicm is the common-mode gain. Both are dimensionless, and each is measured with the other input component held at zero.

For a differential output, let vo1 and vo2 be the two collector voltages. The differential output is vod = vo1 − vo2, in volts; the common-mode output is voc = (vo1 + vo2)/2, in volts. Then vod = Ad vid + A_cm-dm vicm, where Ad = vod/vid is the differential gain and A_cm-dm = vod/vicm is the common-mode-to-differential gain. In a perfectly symmetric pair A_cm-dm = 0, because common-mode input appears equally at both collectors: it cancels in vod and shows up only in voc.

Use magnitudes when comparing gains, because either gain can be negative. For a BJT pair with collector resistors RC and a tail resistance REE, a single-ended output at one collector gives Ad = gm RC/2 and Acm ≈ −RC/(2REE). gm is the small-signal transconductance of each transistor, in A/V; RC is the collector resistor, in Ω; REE is the small-signal resistance of the tail, in Ω. The minus sign means a rise in common-mode input lowers that collector. A larger REE reduces |Acm|; an ideal tail current source has REE → ∞ and Acm → 0. With a differential output, perfect symmetry cancels common mode and the residual is set by mismatch, through A_cm-dm.
Ad = gm RC/2,   Acm ≈ −RC/(2REE),   CMRR ≈ REE/re
blocks.where: Single-ended output at one collector. gm is small-signal transconductance in A/V; RC is the collector resistor in Ω; REE is the tail small-signal resistance in Ω; re is the small-signal emitter resistance of each BJT in Ω, with re ≈ 1/gm. The last expression uses gm REE = REE/re.

blocks.text: CMRR, the common-mode rejection ratio, is the ratio of the two gains: CMRR = |Ad/Acm|. In decibels, CMRRdB = 20 log10 |Ad/Acm|. The 20 is used because Ad and Acm are voltage gains. A CMRR of 80 dB means |Ad/Acm| = 10^(80/20) = 10^4. For a differential output, replace Acm by A_cm-dm in these ratios. A fractional mismatch δ = ΔRC/RC between the two collector resistors converts common-mode input into a differential output. To a first approximation |A_cm-dm/Ad| ≈ δ/(gm REE), so CMRR ≈ gm REE/δ = (REE/re)/δ. A 1% mismatch with REE/re = 4000 gives CMRR ≈ 400,000, or about 112 dB. Matched resistors and transistor pairs therefore matter. Common-mode input range is the range of vicm over which the pair still works: input transistors stay in the active region and the tail current source has enough voltage. Outside it, bias current changes or devices saturate, and CMRR collapses. In a fully differential amplifier, a common-mode feedback (CMFB) loop senses the average of the two outputs and adjusts a bias so that output average stays at a chosen reference. Measurement of op-amp CMRR is in 5.6.

blocks.where: Ad is differential-mode gain; Acm is common-mode gain; CMRR is the common-mode rejection ratio, dimensionless; CMRR<sub>dB</sub> is in decibels. For a differential output, use A_cm-dm in place of Acm.

figure.caption: Inputs 1.010 V and 0.990 V split into a 20 mV difference and a 1.000 V average. The difference is multiplied by 200, the average by 0.02, and the two contributions add at a single-ended output.

spec.title: Splitting inputs into difference and common mode
spec.aria: Block diagram: inputs v1 and v2 are split into a difference vid and an average vicm, which pass through separate gains Ad and Acm before adding at the output.

examples.question: An amplifier has a single-ended output with differential gain Ad = 200 and CMRR = 80 dB. Its inputs are v1 = 1.010 V and v2 = 0.990 V. Find vid, vicm, |Acm|, the differential and common-mode contributions to the output, and the worst-case total output magnitude.
steps: Difference: vid = v1 − v2 = 1.010 V − 0.990 V = 0.020 V = 20 mV.
Differential contribution: Ad vid = 200 × 0.020 V = 4.000 V.
Worst-case total magnitude: |Ad vid| + |Acm vicm| = 4.000 V + 0.020 V = 4.020 V. With opposite signs the magnitude is 4.000 V − 0.020 V = 3.980 V, which is smaller.
examples.answer: The inputs give vid = 20 mV and vicm = 1.000 V; |Acm| = 0.020; the differential contribution is 4.000 V, the common-mode contribution is 0.020 V, and the worst-case total output magnitude is 4.020 V.
examples.check:
Ad = 200.0
cmrr_db = 80.0
v1 = 1.010
v2 = 0.990
vid = v1 - v2
vicm = (v1 + v2) / 2.0
ratio = 10 ** (cmrr_db / 20.0)
Acm = Ad / ratio
v_diff = Ad * vid
v_cm = Acm * vicm
worst = abs(v_diff) + abs(v_cm)
print(f'{vid:.3f}')
print(f'{vicm:.3f}')
print(f'{Acm:.3f}')
print(f'{v_diff:.3f}')
print(f'{v_cm:.3f}')
print(f'{worst:.3f}')

traps: Using vid = v1 + v2 or vicm = v1 + v2: the difference is a subtraction and the common mode is an average.
Using 10 log instead of 20 log for CMRR in dB: gains are voltages, so CMRR<sub>dB</sub> = 20 log10|Ad/Acm|.
Treating CMRR as Ad − Acm: it is a ratio |Ad/Acm|, not a difference.
Using the single-ended Acm formula when the output is taken differentially: perfect symmetry cancels common mode, and mismatch sets the residual.
Forgetting the common-mode input range: a pair can have good small-signal CMRR and still fail when vicm drives the tail current source out of compliance.

quiz.q: Define vid and vicm for inputs v1 and v2.
quiz.a: vid = v1 − v2 in V; vicm = (v1 + v2)/2 in V.

quiz.q: Why is a common-mode signal at both inputs not amplified by an ideal differential pair?
quiz.a: Both base voltages move together, so the tail current and the two collector currents change equally; a differential output sees no change. Only mismatch creates a residual.

quiz.q: Ad = 500, CMRR = 60 dB, vicm = 2.0 V. Find |Acm| and the common-mode output magnitude.
A single-ended BJT pair has REE = 100 kΩ and re = 25 Ω. Estimate CMRR in dB.
A differential-output pair has REE = 100 kΩ, re = 25 Ω, and 1% collector-resistor mismatch. Estimate CMRR in dB.
v1 = 2.005 V and v2 = 1.995 V. Find vid and vicm.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real op-amps, CMRR is measured with a unity-gain buffer and a common-mode step, and it falls with frequency because the input stage's tail impedance and device matching change. Fully differential op-amps and ADCs use common-mode feedback to define the output average; the CMFB loop needs its own stability analysis. Instrumentation amplifiers cascade stages to push CMRR beyond 100 dB for ECG and bridge sensors. Search next for common-mode feedback, CMRR measurement, and resistor trimming in differential amplifiers.
